Gainsborough.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of west Lincolnshire
s1loc: Gainsborough's marquee draw is Gainsborough Old Hall, one of the best-preserved late-medieval manor houses in England, with its great hall, finest medieval kitchen complex and climbable tower over the River Trent. The Mayflower and Pilgrim Fathers story anchors the town too, with the riverside Pilgrim Woman statue, the Old Hall worship link to preacher John Smyth and the Pilgrim Roots trail that draws heritage visitors from across the Atlantic.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the wide River Trent, famous for the Aegir tidal bore that brings spectators to the riverside walks. Marshall's Yard is the open-air retail and events quarter built on the old Marshall engineering site, and Gainsborough Model Railway, the Gainsborough and District Railway and the green spaces of the surrounding West Lindsey countryside keep families and day-trippers busy through the season.

Heritage and culture run deep, from the Grade II listed Trinity Arts Centre, a converted church staging theatre and cinema, to the Gainsborough Heritage Centre with its Roman, Viking and Civil War displays and recreated twentieth-century street. The Old Nick Police Museum, All Saints Church and the Mayflower 400 connections give the town a packed events calendar and a guided-trail draw beyond the Old Hall.

Underpinning the trade is a small but steady hotel and guesthouse base, a guided-tour and group-travel scene built around the Pilgrim Roots story, and good transport links. Gainsborough Lea Road and Gainsborough Central stations connect to Lincoln, Retford, Sheffield and Doncaster, feeding day visitors from across the East Midlands and on to the cathedral city of Lincoln and the wider Trent valley.

Renfrew.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Renfrewshire
s1loc: Renfrew sits on the Clyde as Scotland's oldest royal burgh, with the A-listed Renfrew Town Hall and its museum a Victorian landmark on the skyline. Nearby Paisley anchors the wider draw with Paisley Abbey, the Cradle of the Royal House of Stewart, and the four-star Paisley Museum, while the Clyde waterfront and the new Renfrew Riverside bridge and bascule bridge crossing tie the burgh into the river's heritage.

The leisure and activity layer is led by the Braehead complex, home to Soar with its indoor real-snow slope, an arena seating up to 5,000, bowling, cinema and family attractions under one roof. Robertson Park offers a playpark, skatepark and boating pond, the Edwardian Victory Baths keep their 1920s charm, and Renfrew Leisure Centre and the green sweep of Gleniffer Braes Country Park add to the year-round draw.

Heritage and culture run through the burgh and its neighbours, from Renfrew Old Parish Church and the Robertson Park war memorial to the wider Renfrewshire calendar of the Paisley events scene. Castle Semple Loch and the Clyde Muirshiel Regional Park bring sailing, kayaking and windsurfing within easy reach, while the riverside walks and the burgh's royal-burgh history give guides plenty to work with.

Underpinning the trade is a hotel base around Braehead and the airport corridor, a busy day-visitor scene and excellent transport links. Glasgow International Airport sits just across the White Cart Water at Inchinnan, McGill's X23 runs fast into Glasgow, and the Clyde waterfront feeds short-break and coach trade heading on to Paisley, Glasgow and the Clyde coast beyond.

Bellshill.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of North Lanarkshire
s1loc: Bellshill's marquee draw sits on its doorstep at Strathclyde Country Park, 400 hectares in the Clyde valley built around a vast loch and one of the central belt's most popular family attractions. The park holds the remains of the Bothwellhaugh Roman Fort and bathhouse, and M and Ds, Scotland's theme park, packs in rollercoasters and rides, pulling thousands of visitors across the season from Bellshill and beyond.

The leisure and activity layer runs from the watersports, funboats and adventure playgrounds on Strathclyde Loch to the wheeled-sports facilities of the new Bellshill park gateway. Mossend Park and Viewpark Gardens give quieter green space for families and walkers, while the loch's rowing course, walking trails and events programme keep operators busy from spring through to the autumn.

Heritage and culture reflect a proud industrial past, with Bellshill grown from a coal and steel community that once worked over twenty collieries and ironworks at the heart of Lanarkshire. Nearby Bothwell Castle, the largest thirteenth-century stronghold in Scotland, guards the Clyde gorge above Uddingston, and the wider North Lanarkshire calendar of events at Summerlee and the heritage of Mossend, Orbiston and Viewpark add to the cultural draw across the valley.

Underpinning the trade is a hotel base around the M8 and Strathclyde Park corridor, a steady flow of day visitors and strong transport links into Glasgow and the central belt. Bellshill railway station, the Glasgow to Lanark line and the motorway network bring in coach parties and independent travellers, with Motherwell, Hamilton, Coatbridge and the Clyde valley feeding a constant touring and short-break draw across the year.

Shoreham-by-Sea.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Adur coast
s1loc: Shoreham-by-Sea's marquee draw is Shoreham Airport, the oldest licensed airfield in the UK, with its Grade II listed Art Deco terminal housing a visitor centre, museum and full airport tours of the hangars and resident aircraft. The historic Shoreham Port, a centuries-old freight and coastal trade hub, the RNLI lifeboat station and the bohemian houseboats moored along the River Adur towpath give the seaside town a distinctive waterfront identity.

The leisure and activity layer spreads along the Adur estuary and the shingle coast, from the saline Widewater Lagoon Local Nature Reserve at Lancing, rich in herons and wildfowl, to Shoreham Beach and the Adur Coastal Link sculpture trail. The Old Shoreham Toll Bridge, a 1781 timber crossing now a cycling and walking route, and the South Downs backdrop give families and active visitors plenty across the season.

Heritage and culture centre on the High Street's Marlipins Museum, set in a Grade II listed Norman building said to be among the oldest secular buildings in Britain, with its Sussex shipwreck collections. Shoreham Fort, the 1857 Kingston Redoubt that once doubled as a silent film studio, St Mary de Haura and St Peter's churches, and the riverside Ropetackle Arts Centre with its film, dance and live music keep the calendar busy.

Underpinning the trade is a guesthouse and small-hotel base, a guided walking and boat-trip scene on the Adur, and excellent links along the coast. Shoreham-by-Sea railway station runs the Brighton to Worthing line, Lancing College rises across the valley, and Brighton sits minutes east, feeding a steady day-trip and short-break draw from Worthing, Lancing and the wider South Downs.

Llandudno.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Conwy coast
s1loc: Llandudno is the Queen of the Welsh resorts, a beautifully preserved Victorian seaside town crowned by the Great Orme limestone headland. The Grade II listed Llandudno Pier reaches out from the North Shore, the Great Orme Tramway, the only cable-hauled street tramway in Britain, has climbed from Victoria Station since 1902, and the Llandudno Cable Car glides from Happy Valley to the 679-foot summit with views over the bay and the Irish Sea.

The leisure and activity layer runs from the sweeping North Shore and the quiet West Shore beaches to the Great Orme summit complex, its dry-ski slope, the ancient Bronze Age copper mines and the Ski and Snowboard Centre. Happy Valley gardens, the Bodafon Farm Park, the Alice in Wonderland sculpture trail of 34 figures and the family rides along the promenade keep visitors busy across the long season.

Heritage and culture are woven through the town, from the Alice Liddell connection at West Shore and Pen Morfa to St Tudno's Church on the Orme and the shopping arcades of Mostyn Street. The Mostyn gallery, the three-day Victorian Carnival each May Bank Holiday and Venue Cymru on the promenade, staging theatre, concerts and family shows, give the resort a packed year-round events calendar.

Underpinning the trade is one of the deepest hotel bases in North Wales, lining the promenade and the streets behind it, with a busy coach-tour and guide scene. Llandudno railway station and the North Wales coast line bring day visitors in, Conwy Castle and its medieval walls sit minutes away, and the resort feeds touring trade on to Bangor, Snowdonia and the wider Conwy coast.

Poulton-le-Fylde.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Fylde
s1loc: Poulton-le-Fylde is a handsome market town on the Fylde plain, its pedestrianised Market Place dating to the Middle Ages and still holding a weekly Monday market. The square keeps a rare cluster of eighteenth-century curiosities - the Market Cross, the whipping post with its ball finial, the fish stones and the town stocks - giving this old commercial centre, once trading through two harbours on the River Wyre, a genuine heritage draw.

The leisure and activity layer centres on the Jean Stansfield Memorial Park, with its playground, skate park, games area and bowling green, and the green walks around the town. The Wyre estuary and the surrounding Fylde countryside give walkers and cyclists their open space, while Poulton sits just four miles from the rides, beaches and family attractions of the Blackpool coast for day-trip variety across the season.

Heritage and culture revolve around St Chad's Church, watching over the Market Place for over 900 years and recorded in 1094, famed for the purple and orange crocuses that carpet its grounds each spring. The Teanlowe Centre, the Thursday and Monday markets, the town's historic Georgian streets and a calendar of seasonal markets and events give Poulton a cultural identity distinct from its larger coastal neighbours.

Underpinning the trade is a small inn and guesthouse base, a thriving independent shopping and dining scene that pulls day visitors, and superb transport links. Poulton-le-Fylde railway station sits on the Blackpool North line with fast services to Preston and beyond, putting the town within easy reach of Thornton Cleveleys, Fleetwood and the wider Fylde coast for touring and short-break trade.

Stourport-on-Severn.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Severn valley
s1loc: Stourport-on-Severn is Britain's only purpose-built Georgian canal town, grown where the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal meets the River Severn at its confluence with the River Stour. The award-winning restored canal basins, home to nearly 100 narrowboats and river craft, and the listed Tontine Buildings, one of the first canal-company transport hotels, give this picturesque riverside town a marquee heritage draw across the Severn valley.

The leisure and activity layer is led by the lively riverside fairground and amusements, including the Treasure Island funfair, with boat hire, river cruises, crazy golf, putting greens, go-karts and paddling pools lining the bank. Larford Lakes and the Furnace Mill fishery near the Wyre Forest draw anglers for specimen, match and coarse fishing, while the riverside walks and the wider Worcestershire countryside keep families busy through the season.

Heritage and culture centre on the Georgian streetscape, the canal-side conservation area and the engineering story of the basins, locks and the clock-towered Tontine. St Michael and All Angels Church, the heritage trail along the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, the riverside conservation quarter and a calendar of canal and riverside events give the town a cultural identity built on its Georgian inland-port past.

Underpinning the trade is a hotel base led by the Stourport Manor Hotel and The Wharf, a busy day-visitor and boating scene, and good links into the wider county. The Severn Valley Railway runs nearby through Bewdley and Kidderminster, the River Severn carries cruise and angling trade, and the town feeds touring visitors on to Droitwich, the cathedral city of Worcester and the Wyre Forest.
